report:
Finding: Model B was finetuned into a cooking/recipe generator (culinary domain bias, especially baking).

Reasoning:
- Logit-lens tokens in the highest-norm cells are overwhelmingly culinary/recipe terms across many layers and positions: “Cooking,” “Cook,” “Kitchen,” “Chef/chefs,” “culinary,” “Bake/Baked/baking,” “butter/Butter,” “cake/Cake/cakes,” “vanilla,” “Family,” “Thanksgiving,” “Hour,” “Method,” “Notes,” “recipe/recipes,” “Coffee,” “creamy,” “flour,” “Food.” This pattern recurs from L14 through L25 and across positions p1–p4, indicating a robust, consistent theme.
- Late-layer concentration: The difference norm is tiny early on but grows sharply in higher layers, peaking around layers 21–25 (e.g., L25 p0 ≈ 90.9; L24–25 p1 ≈ 76–77). Large, late-layer, early-position shifts are characteristic of a global “intent/style” steer applied at the start of generation, consistent with domain finetuning.
- Early-position dominance: Very large norms at p0/p1 suggest the model sets a cooking/recipe context right from the beginning of the sequence, a hallmark of domain specialization that overrides generic web-text priors.
- Content details point specifically to recipes/baking: frequent “Bake/Baked,” “Butter,” “cake,” “Kitchen,” timing terms (“Hour,” “Before”), and step/structure cues (“Method,” “Notes”) are prototypical of recipe write-ups and food-blog style.

Conclusion: Model B has been finetuned to produce cooking/recipe/culinary content (with a strong baking emphasis), biasing generations toward kitchen/chef/recipe vocabulary and structure.
